utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome back, Mr. Djordjevic. We are about to move to the next witness. Could I mention a matter in respect of the decision of the Chamber concerning the witness, that is our decision of the 22nd of January. There was a slippage between paragraphs 13 and 14. In paragraph 13 we identified paragraphs 16 to 19 as not admissible. In the following paragraph we failed to make again the reference to paragraphs 16 to 19 in line 5. We identified paragraphs 9, 11, 14, that is, 11 to 14, but we did not mention again 16 to 19, and they should have been mentioned there. I hope that that has not produced any confusion or misunderstanding because of the clear reference in paragraph 13, but I think it's best that it be identified and corrected now. We could have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not redacted the witness statement in this precise way, but we take upon ourselves to do that during the weekend so that everything is put in order. That is all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you. If you would read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you. Are the earphones not fitting you suitably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're suitable. Everything is fine, just for me to adjust a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the interpreter that my surname is Djordjevic and not Djurdjic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you some questions now as part of the Defence case for our client. Let me first ask you for your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of December, 1947, in Hum, municipality of Nis, Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. I would now like to ask you, have you made a statement beforehand in Belgrade to a certain investigator who was there to ask you for such a statement, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did make a statement for the proceedings of Mr. Milutinovic et al. in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a statement of the 23rd of August, 2007?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court usher, as has already been the practice in this case, to provide the witness a hard copy of the documents we will be showing him. So could those documents be given to the witness in a binder so that Mr. Petkovic can look at the statement and confirm that that is the statement that he made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you provided such a binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the document, it is marked with the number 1 in the binder before you. The statement is from the 23rd of August, 2007, and it says that Mr. Ratko Djukanovic, investigator, took this statement from you. Is that that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Petkovic, would you add or change anything in this statement, or would you abide by that statement today, would you say absolutely the same as you said then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that some paragraphs have been darkened, but as far as I can see at first glance I wouldn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, this is the decision of this Trial Chamber that certain things are unacceptable in this statement, either because they express an expert opinion or because they are irrelevant portions of the statement that do not apply to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in the narrow sense. So you absolutely agree that this is the statement you gave to the investigator in 2007 and that you are familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the observations that I just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard from you that you gave this statement as a witness in the case against Milutinovic and others. In the binder at the end you will find a transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic case. Did you review this statement before coming here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: After I was informed that I should come to be a witness in this case, I did review and listened also to the transcript; and it is faithful to what I actually said. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What you find before you in the binder, the transcript, you can confirm that that is what you actually said during your testimony in the Milutinovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: If it is identical to what I heard and reviewed, then it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness statement is marked D011-1661, and the transcript is marked D010-2503. So I would like to tender the witness statement and which we will redact over -- during the weekend, and I will put it in the e-court. And also for this transcript to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The best course would appear, Mr. Djordjevic, to be that the statement will for the moment be marked for identification until you've been able to make the complete redaction, and it will then become an exhibit so that there's no confusion about what is admissible. And the transcript of evidence in the Milutinovic trial will be received immediately as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement will be Exhibit D00512, marked for identification; and the transcript will be Exhibit D00513.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall now present a brief summary of what the witness will be testifying about today. When the NATO forces attack started against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the witness was chief of the administration of the land forces of the Army of Yugoslavia. And during the aggression and the bombing he was in the staff of the Supreme Command as chief of the ABHO in the department for ground forces. The witness will testify that at the beginning of 1999 during preparations and elaboration of plans for defence against NATO, the Yugoslav Army undertook steps to intensify training in the area of AB -- nuclear, biological, and chemical defence, and especially with respect to protective masks and providing information as to the location of weapons with uranium -- depleted uranium in the vicinity of Skopje. The witness will testify that immediately after the beginning of the NATO aggression ammunition began to be used with depleted uranium. The witness will testify that the NATO leadership denied the use of such ammunition with depleted uranium within the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A long time after the aggression, the NATO staff in February 2000 admitted that the use of ammunition with depleted uranium during the aggression -- the NATO submitted a report with the locations that were bombed in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the experts for depleted uranium on the 21st of September, 2000, in Geneva. The witness will explain that the effects of the use of this type of ammunition against personnel and civilians are fatal because of contamination. The witness will testify that the use of depleted uranium ammunition in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is a violation of the basic principles of international humanitarian law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Djordjevic. Yes, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think the summary -- if the summary is correct, the same type of expert testimony that was the subject of our 92 -- of your 92 ter decision seems to be planned to come in in testimony. So I'm just a little concerned about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The concern expressed, Mr. Djordjevic, is that something you are saying in your summary is going to be inconsistent with our ruling in respect of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can share your concern but stress to assure that the Defence in the direct examination will not overstep the limits set by the Trial Chamber. What we will be asking the witness will be within the framework of his personal knowledge as a person who was directly responsible for protecting military personnel and also the population and the inhabitants, the civilians. That was what the witness has been doing all his life. We will not ask him for an expert opinion because he is not an expert, but we will ask him what he knows about the measures to protect against the nuclear, biological, and chemical radiation, and this was his field of work until his retirement. Your fear that I will go beyond the limits, that I will be asking him questions about medicine and the consequences on the population, I assure you that I will not be asking any such questions. And should you think that I have turned a deaf ear to the decision of the Trial Chamber, I will immediately stop and act in accordance with your directions and rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two observations follow, Mr. Djordjevic. It appears that your summary may be going beyond the scope of what is contemplated in our decision, and if in that respect you are intending by oral evidence to lead matters that we have excluded from the summary, clearly that is going to be the subject of controversy and decision here. So it should not be included in the summary at this point. I said there were two points, but I think I've wrapped them together. We will look with great care if it is that you think you've found a way of getting around what was our decision. So we will not -- you will understand at the moment that we cannot give you any direction beyond our decision, but if the course of the evidence exposes difficulties, you would expect that they will have to be the subject of further deliberation and decision. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me conclude this summary by saying that the witness will testify the use of cluster bombs and explain in connection with the use of such cluster bombs that these are not explicitly prohibited, but that they certainly represent a violation of certain rights envisaged by international conventions if they are properly interpreted. Finally, the witness will testify that NATO forces bombed the territory of the Federal Republic, and thereby also Kosovo and Metohija, destroyed industrial installations. I will leave out number 1.000 from the summary because it is in English and because it applies to the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Chamber has insisted that we limit our remarks to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In more than 60 per cent of cases, the targets were civilian ones, very frequently inhabited areas, and depleted uranium ammunition and cluster bombs were used, though they were aware of the effects of such ammunitions. That would briefly be the summary, with my additional observation that I'm quite prepared to respect the decisions of the Chamber taken on the 22nd of January should I go beyond the scope envisaged by that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I see again on your feet, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I really don't mean to interrupt at this stage. I just, so we can avoid problems later, to clarify. Further in the summary Mr. Djordjevic just stated an intent that this witness will testify that basically what NATO did was a violation of conventions. And I think that's giving a legal opinion. That's more expert testimony, and that's something that would cause the Prosecution concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment your concern is that the witness in the evidence indicated by Mr. Djordjevic should not go beyond expressing what he knows about the weapons that may have been used and not go so far as to say because of those weapons there was or may have been a violation of international conventions. Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you absorbed that, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. But 90 per cent of the people who as soldiers were tried at this court were not experts in international law just because of that, because they could not detect and identify -- because they had not been taught that since schools. Here we have before us a general of the JNA, and of course the Bench will rule and decides on the basis of the facts that they're going to hear from the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm retired general of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you retired?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: At the 31st of March, 2000 -- 2002 I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, could you go through your education, when did you enter the VJ, and could you please explain your path through the educational system without my questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from grammar school, I enrolled in the military academy of the land forces in Belgrade. For the first two years I studied general subjects in Belgrade. Year three and four I went to study in Krusevac. At the time it was an educational centre of the JNA on nuclear, biological, and chemical defence, and apart from other activities, that centre trained future experts in NBC defence. And to avoid this dilemma, whether we knew anything about this or not, let me tell you that we studied physics, chemistry, some elements of medicine, four or five types of chemistries, and military subjects in terms of detection, dosimetry, detection of radiological materials, which means that I am competent to answer questions put to me in this respect. As far as how my testimony will be taken by the Bench, the Judges, it is up to them. After graduating from the academy, I also attended technical and military academy in Zagreb, chemical course, and I graduated from the military staff college and war college of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You went quite integrated deal of detail what your education was like, but what did you do as a professional soldier? Did you spend your whole career as a JNA officer, or did you have some other activities? If you worked exclusively in the JNA, could you please specify what you worked on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the academy, I performed basic duties, commandeering a platoon, commanding a company. I was Chief of Staff of the regiment and the chief of the NBC defence personnel. After I graduated from staff college, I was in the command of the 1st Army, head of the NBC defence service. After that duty, I was transferred and appointed as chief of the NBC defence in the General Staff of the VJ. After that I was transferred to the federal defence ministry, where I was assistant minister for civil defence, and that also concerns the protection and rescue of civilians. And in my capacity I was linked between the VJ and Ministry of Defence and civilians. We worked on decontaminating the areas contaminated by depleted uranium in the territory of southern Serbia. After my professional career ended, I have been active in working on issues of depleted uranium munitions. I'm one of the lobbyists who advocates to cleanse the area of Kosovo and Metohija from depleted uranium because it presents a grave danger for those who work and live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petkovic, in your military career did you do anything else apart from NBC defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. As you can judge from what I said, I mainly performed tasks from within that area, and my career in the ministry was connected to this area. And this is why I went to the defence ministry, to be a liaison officer between that ministry and the civilians, particularly seeing what was going on during the war and after seeing the aftermath and the consequences of such bombings and such munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you when -- which position did you hold when NATO launched its aggression against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Before it started in 1997, I'd been appointed head of the administration for NBC defence at the General Staff of the VJ, and this is the post I occupied when NATO started its aggression against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: During the war until June, did you remain on that post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: When the bombing started I was in the headquarters of the Supreme Command Staff, I was head of the administration for NBC defence in the land forces, so I was informed about all matters and developments concerning my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's retrieve D006-3372, the B/C/S version, and in English if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in your binder this document appears under tab 2 in English. Thank you. Can you see the date here? It's -- apparently the document dates from 1999, but before the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 5th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Two weeks before the start, before 24th of March, 1999. Do you know, General, sir, anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is familiar -- I'm familiar with it. I drafted it, and my then-superior officer, assistant chief of land forces within the General Staff, General Panic, signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is it all about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had intelligence that NATO forces in their arsenals possessed depleted uranium munitions, and that those munitions had been used in Iraq. By this document we sought, for the purposes of assessments of the land forces, the intelligence service of the General Staff should collect intelligence whether the forces of NATO that had been deployed in Macedonia and were readying themselves for the upcoming attack, whether they possessed depleted uranium munitions. And this table shows the different types of munitions that contained depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, this table - if we could zoom in on it, please, in both versions --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This table is an overview of calibres, types of weapons, and the contents of depleted uranium. For instance, you see here that Bradley machine-gun, that's 25-millimetre cannon, contained 85 grams of depleted uranium. Then guns on A-10 aircraft, they contain munitions with 300 grams. Then 105-millimetre guns mounted on tanks have munitions containing the respective masses of depleted uranium, including guns, tanks, Abrams. Those were used by US forces in Iraq; we had intelligence on that. So we wanted confirmation whether the troops being readied, if land invasion were to be effected, would they use such munitions so that we could prepare NBC defence for the military personnel and civilians throughout Serbia, but also in Kosovo and Metohija because the focus of that operation was Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In respect to this document, could you explain the claim in the penultimate paragraph. There's reference made of forces deployed in the territory of Macedonia, et cetera. Did you have any intelligence as high-ranking military officer who was engaged in NBC defence about such matters? Is it why your colleagues mentioned those forces in Macedonia? What was supposed to mean? Let's avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the General Staff of the VJ, I had information that the troops that were possibly effect land operations against Kosovo would be concentrated in Macedonia, and that their introduction into Kosovo and Metohija was being planned through Macedonia. Because this -- this area contained the best terrain for tanks to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And this was why this reference is made here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's please take a look at page 2, it's D006-3373 is the marking on the page and in the English version as well, please. Please take a look at page 1, General, sir. Are you familiar with the -- with this document, the letter-head, et cetera? But before you answer that, may the usher show page 2 of this document, keep it on the screen for a while, then page 3 of the document, and finally the fourth page containing the signature. Thank you. Let's go to page 3, please. And finally, page 4, containing the signature and the seal and the rubber stamp. I think -- yes, the English version has one page more. Thank you. Mr. Petkovic, are you familiar with this document and whether this person who signed, do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a confidential document 77-1 from the 12th of July, 1997. I signed it. I drafted it. There is a number of such documents of that nature aimed at familiarising the subordinate unit with the type of ammunition that would be used if the aggression were to be effected, because in our training we had not trained a lot on such matters because it wasn't part of our curriculum, but since we expected depleted uranium munitions to be used in the future we felt the need to inform our subordinate units about the types of munitions, the consequences of such munitions if used, and we prepared an instruction - and this is an excerpt from such instructions - on what to do if such munitions really come to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: General, you spoke and wrote about the characteristics of such munitions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you wrote about the danger that this ammunition represented in terms of military doctrine and what you were in charge of in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you dealt with the characteristics of such munitions, we saw that table --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- what were the sources of your information that you disseminated among subordinated units, since you said you expected an attack with such munitions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Basic source of information that depleted uranium munitions was used in the territory of former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was the report of an expert panel including people from the NBC defence staff in 1997, and I was part of that administration, who went in 1995 to the territory of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina, where NATO forces had used depleted uranium munitions when bombing the area of Hadzici and some other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Large quantities of such munitions were found, collected, and brought to the Vinca institute where they were analysed, and it was uncontestably [as interpreted] determined that it went for depleted uranium munitions, and a recommendation was then issued on how to proceed with such munitions. This -- so the first source was the expert group analysis that I had in my hands and I read. And of course being a professional in the field, I studied literature about such munitions, some reference books; then over the internet, in the press, I could find some articles about depleted uranium munitions since it was used in Iraq. There were a plethora of articles about the munitions, how it was used. There were texts about the illnesses which followed from the use of depleted uranium munitions, about conflicts in certain Western European armies, Italy, France, Great Britain, whose personnel served in Iraq and who fell ill. And the suspicion was that being in an area which was bombed with depleted uranium munitions was one of the reasons why they fell ill. There was some -- certain commissions to determine and look into the matter of people returning from Iraq and Bosnia-Herzegovina following in and trying to find the link between their sojourn there and illness, and since I was person responsible for that, in the General Staff I studied all such sources, so to be prepared for what was awaiting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So this -- your actions were preventative actions in terms of what was expected and what ultimately did happen. But a connected document to this is under tab 3 in your binder, and it's already been admitted as D174. I propose, since it is a logical consequence of my line of questioning that first we admit the document that we discussed with the witness, and then of course the one that has already been admitted I will seek that witness speak about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does not the document contain precisely the matter that Ms. Petersen was raising? I've not had an opportunity to study it, merely to glance very quickly as it was run through on e-court, but I thought I identified. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document that preceded everything that happened and is a reflection of the preventive activities of the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia in that direction, the document can be considered fully relevant or irrelevant depending on its contents. But that is why I asked the witness to comment on this document, whether he had compiled it, what the sources were. We heard that this was a finding of a group of experts, therefore, not his own findings. And you said that those could not be used. And because of this, I thought that the document was relevant, and I don't think it could in any way violate the ruling of the Chamber. Of course if the Chamber decides otherwise, it can be marked for identification and then the Chamber can subsequently decide what should be done with it. But I think it should not cause any problems because these -- this document contains the factual description of the ammunition and that was his task. And it would not be logical in view of what was happening in his country for him not to have carried out his task in this way. These data about ammunition are accessible on any site of NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. Our problem is that I'm not clear what document you're referring to. There was one document which identified in a single page a number of possible types of ammunition that might be used, a document from early 1999. Is that the document to which you are presently referring, or is it the next document? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two documents form a single one in the e-court, and they have been marked as I have just said. This is what my assistant tells me. But both documents represent a logical whole, reflecting the activities of this officer of the VJ before the war that occurred in the territory of the former FRY and in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I find that I cannot immediately identify what I saw earlier, Mr. Djordjevic. I'm going to ask for the -- I think the best shot may be to mark it for identification and give us time to look at it, but I see that Ms. Petersen is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think you're correct in identifying problems in the second part of this document. If you look at page 4, it does give expert testimony on the chemistry and properties of depleted uranium, and this is exactly the subject of the 92 ter ruling. I think going into detail about his underlying sources and his qualifications is not the point; the point is this person was not noticed as an expert witness. The expert witness procedures haven't been followed. So whether he's qualified, whatever his source are, this still should not be admitted. One option could be to admit this for the limited purpose of showing that this was something that he sent out, but not for the truth of some of the assertions and the content within the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Until we have had an opportunity to consider the document, it's not appropriate for us to attempt a ruling. We will have it marked for identification; and in view of the submissions that you have made and any further that may need to be made in the course of the evidence, we will come to the view about admissibility of, I suspect, part of the document rather than the whole of it. It will be marked for identification. They should be marked separately. While they may be in e-court as one exhibit, they are in time and nature quite different and they will be considered quite separately. So there should be two different numbers given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document bearing document number D006-3372 will be Exhibit D00514 marked for identification; and the second document starting with D006-3373 will be Exhibit D00515, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I continue with the examination of this witness, I have to deal with a procedural dilemma that I personally have. My understanding of the Chamber's ruling was a ruling which says that the witness shouldn't be heard here as an expert because he's not an expert, he's a witness. And as a witness, I thought that he would speak about his own knowledge as a person in charge of this particular type of protection of personnel and civilians. So my question now is: I know that he cannot speak as an expert or maybe not even what he did before the Chamber made his ruling. Could this cause the concern of the Chamber that the witness engaged in something that he shouldn't have done, and in his report he's not referring to his own knowledge but to the knowledge of the institute in Vinca. We will ask him what the Vinca institute is, and I believe the Chamber knows that. So he's not speaking as an expert; he's speaking about what he learned as an official of the state who gathered the necessary opinions and information. If you feel that we should not hear any of this, I will be guided by your decision, but I don't wish to be in a dilemma anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is following a course which is attempting to give to the Defence as much scope as possible to present what it sees to be relevant. What we are dealing with now, the subject matter, is a long way from the centre of the issues concerning this accused. There is no question of his involvement in any form of depleted uranium or other nuclear weaponry or munitions. There seems to be some general appreciation of relevance on the part of the Defence that the nature of the conduct of NATO had some relevance to the actions of the accused. Now, at the moment we're trying to give you as much scope as possible to advance that. Understand that as a preliminary observation, because on some views the whole of this subject could be seen to be irrelevant, but we're not taking that view at the moment. The witness, so far as his knowledge and experience and activities are relevant to our case, will be allowed to give evidence of that. The fact that in the course of his activities he may have come into contact with some area of expertise and be aware of what an expert body has done or concluded, A, does not make this man an expert in that subject; B, does not make the indirect evidence of this witness admissible about that subject matter of expertise. It's one thing what this witness ordinarily does and what he did and what he can tell us about that. When he comes to expressing conclusions, as the document before us does, when he comes to trying to say: Well, the conclusion of an expert institute was A, B, and C, he is moving into the field of expertise. And that is the area where we are not prepared to accept evidence. Now, is that an indication enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, but my understanding was that he shouldn't be the one who testifies, but if he says that he received it from an institute this is just a simple fact which we can accept or not. I shall nevertheless try to explain to the Chamber through the direct examination why this will be relevant, particularly for this case and the indictment against this accused. So allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have here a document. Could it be placed on the e-court marked for D006-3384. Could you please show us the last page. Could we have the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, this is tab 4 in your binder. Could you just tell us briefly whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do recognise the document. It was compiled in my command, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does this document represent, what is the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was compiled on the 4th of May, 1999, in view of the fact that there was the possibility of a land operation being launched. We felt it necessary on the basis of the information we had received of various types and calibres of munitions, for guns with depleted uranium, and therefore as part of measures against ABHO we felt it necessary to instruct subordinated units with the characteristics of these munitions as part of measures to protect and remove the consequences should this ammunition be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask you anything more about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should also like to tender this document into evidence, and it discusses the facts of the ammunitions being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there's the same problem, if you particularly look at the last paragraph of this. And I'm not sure the exact solution because I would concede that this is admissible for a limited purpose, of showing that this was something that was sent out by the General. However, the facts contained in that last paragraph are, you know, an expert opinion. And so we would state that this should not be considered for the truth of that content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it an issue in this case, in the view of the Defence, Mr. Djordjevic, that it is a question whether members of the forces of the FRY were informed that there may be weapons of this nature used against them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have asked one of the questions that will be the subject of my next question, but I don't mind if the witness answers that question straight away because it is part of the question I intended to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to move on to the next document. Let this be also marked for identification, and if it is considered to be something that the witness obtained about technical characteristics that any child can find on the internet and is considered an expert report -- specifically I found this same information on some 50.000 or so pages on the internet about these munitions. But let the Chamber rule about this. I wouldn't keep the Chamber in discussing this because it is absolutely common knowledge. But my next question will lead to a solution to this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document presently on the screen, Mr. Djordjevic, will be marked for identification. We will continue then to the next document that you want us to see. If we're able to reach a clear decision as we progress about admissibility, we will do so; but if not, at the end of the evidence when we've got it all and we can look at it fully in the light of any further submissions that you and Ms. Petersen wish to make, we will come to a formal decision about admissibility. So if you could proceed with your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be marked as D00516, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is D006-3401, the English and the B/C/S versions. Could they please be placed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And, General, that would be tab 5 in your binder. You can see that on the screen as well. Please take a look at this document and tell me whether you know what it's all about, and that would be the last string of questions concerning this issue that has been a fountain of contention.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in respect of this document I can tell you the following: NATO forces during their aggression denied the use of depleted uranium munitions, although that was apparent from reports received from VJ units and the efforts that the then-leadership of Yugoslavia was doing to disseminate this information and make it available to official organs. But this was not the case. After the aggression, supported by specific evidence in the field, then the developments of the army -- in the armies who had personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosovo and Metohija because of the health consequences that they suffered, and since the United Nations decided to send a working party from UNEP, this was the so-called group for the Balkans to be sent on a fact-finding mission. And this was the first time that the Secretary-General of NATO on the 17th of January, 2000, officially admits that NATO used depleted uranium munitions in the territory of Serbia, more specifically in the Kosovo and Metohija. And this was prepared by military organs of NATO on the use of depleted uranium munitions during the action of NATO forces. And it says here: "I confirm that DU was used during the Kosovo conflict. They were used -- dropped from A-10 aircraft engaged armoured during Operation Allied Force. It was used throughout the territory of Kosovo on 100 sorties, we recorded 98 of them. 31.000 such rounds was used. According to my information there were more than 50.000. The major focus of these operations was in the area west of the Pec-Djakovica-Prizren highway, in the area surrounding Klisa, in the area around Prizren and in the area in the north of a line joining Suva Reka and Urosevac. But I can tell you that such munitions were used beyond those routes, and it is impossible to indicate precisely every location where DU was used, but for that purpose I am providing a map. And this corroborated our assumption and information on precise location of each DU munition used. They're claiming that it was impossible, and we claimed it was possible, and I believe that VJ information was more precise and more useful. And I hope, finally it says, that this will help UNEP/UNCHS (Habitat) Balkans Task Force in their further work, and this was the first instance when NATO admitted that they had used depleted uranium munitions. In their communique they just indicate the number of sorties, rough number of rounds, and a general indication of the area, but in terms of quantities and the number of locations, they do not match the information that we had which was more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00517, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, in your statement you discuss that PNHBO measures, I think that was paragraph 5 in your statement which has not been redacted. What do you mean by this acronym?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: That would be nuclear, biological, chemical, radiological defence is expert term. This is a set of measures, steps, and actions that individuals and units and commands and officers of all levels should undertake to detect the threat in terms of nuclear, chemical, biological threat and hazard for individuals and the population to be informed about that, for appropriate measures to be taken to eliminate that threat, or consequences to maintain the combat-readiness of units and save the population from possible use of nuclear, biological, chemical weapons or weapons bearing radiological materials, such as depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this respect we took a number of measures, and I'm referring to a number of orders that we issued, which governed the issue of observation, information, reporting to both the civilian population and the army on the imminent threat so that it would be prevented and consequences to the soldiers and population to be reduced. This is why we issued this instruction to all our units in Kosovo and Metohija, laying out in precise terms all these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a consequence of your information, did it affect the conduct of the civilians in the area, of course you did it within the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There were observation posts covering the whole territory and NBC alert was given for the whole territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and of course both soldiers, troops, and civilians were informed of such alerts. Whenever we detected sorties, we would sound sirens. One could identify A-10 aircraft. Each of those sorties was observed in detail. We observed the territory. We determined the state of affairs in certain areas, and marked locations where depleted uranium munitions were used so that people, soldiers, troops, and civilians would not approach such areas. There were such locations close to settlements. It was our duty to notify the population about such threat, and we put up notices, and notices were in Serbian and in Albanian. This was part of the equipment of our units which was then used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the actions of observation and reconnaissance. As a person who was in charge of anti-nuclear and anti-chemical defence and protection, could you please explain the equipment that the troops had to detect the presence of agents. We are talking about radioactivity and radiation in the field and notices and placards being put in Serbian and in Albanian close to settlements. Did you have the equipment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The system and the conception of the defence at the time from the SFRY times and during the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia times was that there was a system that was functioning within the army and there was a system concerning the protection and defence of the civilian population, so-called civil defence. NBC units within the civil defence were connected with army units for nuclear, biological, chemical defence. There were a whole. Everything that the JNA would learn, alternatively civil defence would learn something, they would mutually inform each other. There were NBC units of VJ and NBC units of the defence -- civil defence. They had equipment to detect radioactive emissions in the field. Apart from that VJ units had mobile and stationary radiological labs which could perform quantitative and qualitative tests on samples to obtain the information on the matter being used out in the field, and this is how we obtain such information apart from visual observations, that in the territory in the area of Prizren for the first time on the 30th of March, 1999, depleted uranium munitions were used for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now we are getting into an area that is the subject of our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the intention to interrupt the witness because my next question was going to be -- and of course you will redact whatever you see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question concerned the issue: What is UNEP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: UNEP is an official international organisation of the United Nations, working on protection of the environment. It works within the UN system. Its task is to -- to act wherever there are cases of environmental threats, threats to health, to the population. They issue reports on the basis of fact-finding missions, and prompted by what we discussed just minutes ago, a Balkans group was set up in November 2000 which came to Kosovo and Metohija to gauge the level of detriment to the environment that those preceding developments had caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do not talk about the nature of that report if it exists, but could you indicate, did that agency produce a report on the issue of depleted uranium in Kosovo and Metohija? Please tell us whether it exists or not, whether you know about it or not, without going into the contents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be brief, but let me utter a brief comment on that. That report was produced on the February -- in February of this following year. I read that report. I have my opinion, and if you allow me, I can tell you that it was issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, no. Our interest and the question was solely whether there was a report. I know from what you said earlier that this is a very passionate interest of yours, but you'll understand that we're not here to further the concerns you might have at the moment; we're here to learn just so much of what you know that might help us decide whether the person accused is guilty or not of certain offences. So we have to just stop you at various points in your evidence, and we have the evidence that there is a report on the date that you have indicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the watch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, so am I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- and I think it's the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I didn't know whether you had something a little further you needed to put now, but that not being so we need to have our first break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will continue after the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're going to continue with questions. There won't be too many. I'm going to respect the decision by the Chamber, so I'm going to skip many of the documents that I have here because I believe that what we've already provided is plenty. My following question to you, General, sir, is this: During the combat actions in 1999, did you go to Kosovo? Were you in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in April 1999 I went to Kosovo as part of a team which was touring units of the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did you then only have contacts with the units of the Army of Yugoslavia, or did you also have contacts with the police or some other organs in the Kosovo and Metohija area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The objective of our visits was to tour the units of the VJ and to see what the situation there was and to see what the situation in the field was regarding depleted uranium munitions. So I didn't really have any contacts with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know the accused?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you were visiting Kosovo and Metohija during the war operations in the course of 1999, did you ever see him there personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw him in Kosovo and Metohija. I know him as a police officer. I never had any personal contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us as part of the measures to protect the army and the civilians in Kosovo you carried out certain measures, but also within the SFRY and the FRY system there was something that was called the territorial defence and civilian protection. I assume as a general of the Army of Yugoslavia you are familiar with the defence doctrine of the country, and can you tell us briefly what territorial defence is and what the civilian protection is. Is that one and the same thing, two terms for the same force; or are they two different groups?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Territorial defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territorial defence are units whose task was to protect the territory and the population in that territory. Civilian protection is also a form of protection and rescue in case of accidents, disasters, catastrophes, and their operations cover a given territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My next question is: In view of the fact that you said that these measures that you undertook shortly before NATO attacked the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and which you carried out during the NATO action itself, during the war, that these measures were aimed at specific army units as well as territorial defence and civilian protection. Can you tell us if you noticed whether the population -- there were any migrations of the population during the combat activities at that time. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: During the Supreme Command Staff stay and in other areas of Kosovo and Metohija, we saw that there was migration of the population during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What did this depend on, do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, it depended on the situation in the field, on the combat actions. This had an effect on migration of population from one area to another in Kosovo and Metohija. When it was noticed that there were no rules on the basis of which you could conclude which area would be the next target, the population then set out to leave the Kosovo and Metohija area. They went to Macedonia, Albania, and some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please ask the usher to place on the ELMO document D-1623 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see two maps here. Can you tell me -- first, can you tell me what the first map represents and the second map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Both maps show one and the same situation, but from different sources. The first map is a map drafted in the current Serbia based on information and co-ordinates of places that were struck by depleted uranium munitions. So the top map represents a realistic overview of the quantities of such munition that was dropped in the Kosovo and Metohija area. There were remarks there saying that over 31.000 munitions were --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll stop there. Second map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The second map are probably Western sources, based on NATO information. Contents are more or less the same. Once again, it marks the targets that were hit the most with depleted uranium munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the markings on the first map are and what the markings on the second map are, what are these markings in order to make it clear for the transcript exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can start with the top map and I can say that it contains a marking indicating that a place marked like that is radioactive and it's dangerous, and it should not be approached, and it means that the radioactivity is present there. There is radioactive contamination, and such places should not be approached.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please ask the usher to provide the witness with a marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle on this map that we see here one of those signs, indicating a place that was exposed to depleted uranium ammunition fire.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now zoom in on the second map. I can see that you've circled two such locations on this map that we are looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the bottom map now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will lose the marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We could put both maps on one screen and then have them marked together, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to clarify one thing. The Defence, before it tenders these documents, first we would need to just tender them as MFI documents. Before we tender them, we will need to make a submission in order to be able to deal with this document based on Rule 65 ter. In order to be able to tender this document, these two maps, we will need to do that first. So it's all right that the markings that the witness just made on this map are not saved. I would just like us to look at both maps, and then he can make the markings on one map and the other map, so that we would have information about the places that were marked, what the place marked is on one map and what that is on the other map. So let us look at both maps on the screen at the same time and the witness could on each map mark only one spot that was exposed to depleted uranium munitions fire. I'm doing this because of subsequent questions, where I will explain to the Trial Chamber why we're doing this and what the purpose of that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you circle a location on the top map just once so that we don't have any confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please do the same on the bottom map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: When we look at the first map and the second map, to what extent is the data on the maps identical, the ones from domestic sources and the one from western sources?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information entered later, in September 2000 and what we did after we investigated the terrain and during the combat in Kosovo and Metohija and then after combat activities were completed, it is obvious that the data more or less is the same. There are some inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you here. Would you say that the data is more or less identical?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Which part of Kosovo and Metohija according to these maps was most exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The southern and south-western sectors of Kosovo were exposed the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with this, do you have an explanation why these areas, south and south-western areas of Kosovo and Metohija, were most exposed to this type of fire?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It is my personal view that this territory is -- this area around Prizren, Djakovica, and Pec was bombarded the most with depleted uranium munitions; because according to information that we had, in the event of a land forces operation, the land forces of the NATO Alliance was supposed to be introduced from Albania and from Macedonia. These were the sectors around Djakovica, Prizren, and Pec. So from that territory, the idea was to expel the civilian population and to only leave the units there so that in the event of land forces, the casualties would be reduced and we would in that way avoid condemnation by the international community which would expect a lot of casualties if the civilians had stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were by establishment within the Main Staff, the General Staff, did you have any information about the presence of NATO units in Macedonia and in Albania?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: We did have such data even before the attack was launched, as well as during the attack, that some units or forces were in Albania and Macedonia, specifically relating to the matters that I was dealing with. The data was that the Petrovac airport near Skopje was where a certain quantity of depleted uranium munitions were being stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence for further clarification of what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The maps will be received as one exhibit, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00517, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're coming to the close of the direct examination, so in accordance with your formation duties within the army let me ask you the following: In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, were there any chemical incidents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija facilities were targeted, the destruction of which can be considered a chemical incident. These were warehouses, tanks of chemical products, of crude oil and fuel, and certain chemistry plants, but not to the extent to which these facilities were targeted in Serbia because there weren't that many such installations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information of the use of the so-called cluster bombs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have information that in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija this type of ammunition was used en masse. A classical example is the bombing of the column of Albanian refugees who were returning home after certain period of time, when about 70 or some -- over 70 were killed and about a hundred wounded, and most of them were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that brings to an end the direct examination of this witness, and I would like to thank him for explaining to Your Honours the questions of interest to the Defence. And I will have to tell the Chamber once again that I'm sorry if you thought that I was going to in any way violate the Court's ruling of January. All I did was in -- with the intention of clarifying matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are told that the last exhibit should be 518 and not 517, a numbering error. They are as one marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I must have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not your mistake, Mr. Djordjevic; our mistake. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter whose it is, it's important that we correct it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honours, I need to get a little set up over here once I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, General Petkovic. My name is Paige Petersen. I'll just be asking you a few questions today. So you stated you visited Kosovo in April of 1999. Other than that, where were you physically stationed during the war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was stationed in the Supreme Command Staff, in the facility where the Supreme Command Staff was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, can you just please clarify physically where that is located.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why that is important for me to say this. According to establishment, an appropriate facility was used and it was outside Kosovo and Metohija, and it was in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, unless there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that sufficient for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I -- if he -- I guess I don't need the specific address, but if he could give the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've actually had it from other leading army witnesses, but I respect the General's concern not to say it for security reasons. The important thing is it was not in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was not in Kosovo. It was on the territory of Serbia. If you're interested in any further detail, ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. First I'd like to look at the last exhibit that you were talking about, and I'm sorry, I'm not sure if it was given an exhibit number. It was -- okay, I'm told that it was 518.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, so I just would like to clarify. On this map you're saying this is where depleted uranium was found or this is where radioactive material was found subsequent to the war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're speaking of the upper map, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the upper map I told you, during the war and during the bombing of Kosovo and Metohija, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija there were observation posts for ABH. And within the framework of their activity, they observed the territory and noted down the strikes by A-10 planes using depleted uranium ammunitions. You know that A-10 planes have a 30-millimetre gun, and in one sortie - and this was visible by somebody on the observation post - this was a sign that fire from that gun was using depleted uranium. And after the ending of the bombing and the end of the air-strikes and danger from air-strikes, there were reconnaissance patrols who went to the area; and using appropriate means for radiological detection and dosimetrics, measured whether there was any radioactivity there or not. If there was any radioactivity, then they would mark that location on the map indicating the co-ordinates, and in subsequent reports those co-ordinates were sent to the appropriate commands. And that is how we established these co-ordinates. This was done and marked on the maps after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So -- so would you agree that this basically shows where there were the heaviest missile strikes that contained depleted uranium? This was the area of the heaviest missile strikes from the A-10s?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These were the locations where strikes were with depleted uranium and places where units established radioactivity. Furthermore, I didn't say a moment ago, the units endeavoured to find remnants of depleted uranium munitions --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: That's okay, sir. I'll stop you there. Thank you for answering my question. I'd like to go back to some of your testimony in the direct examination when you were being questioned by Mr. Djordjevic. This is at page 32, line 17. You stated: "During the Supreme Command Staff stay and in other areas of Kosovo and Metohija, we saw that there was a migration of the population during the war. "Q. What did this depend on, do you have that information? "A. In my opinion, it depended on the situation in the field, on the combat actions." Now, sir, let me ask you: At the time that the war was going on, were you aware that masses of people were leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: While staying in the staff, we did have reports that there were population migrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So this was reported to you in the Supreme Command Staff, that there was a migration of people from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And were you aware that this involved hundreds of thousands of people from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The extent of my activity and interest in those days did not involve the scope of the migrations. I was just aware that it took place, and as head of the service for ABH I focused on to what extent these strikes can affect the decision of the population to move out. In contact with the inhabitants of Serb ethnicity who fled to the territory of Serbia during and after the war, after my retirement, I heard that fear of the effect of radioactive strikes had forced certain families to flee from Stimlje, Pec, Djakovica to the territory of Serbia. And that was -- and that is one of the factors preventing them from going back to Kosovo because their property is contaminated. And that is why I said at the beginning that I am an advocate --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- regardless of the situation of the area being decontaminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, sir. So you just stated that you spoke with some individuals of Serb ethnicity about why they left Kosovo. How many people did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to members of two or three Serb families. One of them was a very close friend of mine from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware during the time of the war that Kosovo Albanians were leaving from Kosovo from many villages around Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was aware of it. I said a moment ago that a war and any kind of violence encourages migrations from one settlement to another within the framework of one territory - in this case Kosovo. And later on when it became clear that the uncertainty was widespread and that there was danger everywhere, they tended to move to neighbouring countries which were not exposed to the war, and I said Albania, Macedonia, and the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, at the beginning of your testimony you spoke about your transcript from the Milutinovic trial. You recall testifying in this court on 28th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you said today that you'd read this transcript, everything in it is true, and you would say the same things if asked today; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I have read it, or rather, I listened to the audio recording. I would have given a similar answer with a similar meaning. The meaning would be the same. Maybe I wouldn't use the same words.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at that exhibit, D513, and go to page 29 of that transcript, beginning at line 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, General, just to save time, I represent to you that at this point you were being asked about cluster bombs. So that's the context of the following statement. At line 7. "Q. How many struck the civilian -- the population?" Meaning cluster bombs. "A. I cannot say how many, but I can say that that was one of the factors that influenced the mass movement of the population among other things." Now moving down to line 14 Judge Bonomy asked you: "You have done research on this, have you, the movement of the population as a result of the use of cluster bombs? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I did not deal with that particular topic, but I believe that as a soldier my estimation can be relevant, and I stand by what I said that that is one of the factors that could have led to the population movements. People flee planes, bombs. "JUDGE BONOMY: There's no doubt it could have led to that. The question for us whether it did lead to that, which is a different question I think from the one you were answering. "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] If you have more than one answer, then it could have and then putting that together could probably give you the correct answer. "JUDGE BONOMY: Thank you very much. "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] That's as much as I could say." Now General, have you gotten any new information over the last two years about why Albanians left Kosovo other than speaking to a few families who are friends of yours about why they left Kosovo, have you done any research on why Albanians left Kosovo? Any new information since you gave your testimony in Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that my statement then and now coincide, only I said that in the meantime, that is, from the time I testified last time and now, I did have the opportunity to get in contact with certain individuals, to discuss this problem, and the question of the return of refugees. So my answer is: I have not done any research, and I wouldn't discuss that in detail, but it is certainly one of the factors that tends to lead to the population fleeing from various types of ammunitions, bombs, rocketing of certain territories. You must admit that anyone who finds himself in such a territory would flee to the neighbouring village if it hasn't been hit; if it has, then it would move on to some other territory. That is as far as my knowledge goes and my assumptions. Scientifically I have not studied these things, but as an expert for ABH and somebody who warned the army and the civilians of the danger which these documents which have not been admitted into evidence say, that the use of depleted uranium munitions did certainly prompt people to leave because we marked these places with a warning: Do not approach, do not touch. So our advice, our order was that this territory should not be used and the people in that territory should not stay there, they should look for somewhere else. Therefore, my assertion is and I stand by it that the use of depleted uranium munitions in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, in the territory along Prizren, Djakovica, Pec, Stimlje, and other places, because of the danger that the people were aware of because they were warned of the danger was certainly one of the factors that contributed to them leaving that territory or Kosovo and Metohija as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, general, general --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- we now have reports from Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, I need to cut you off at this point. It appears that your opinion on this has gotten much stronger over the last two years. Is that fair to say? If we could just go through this. In Milutinovic when you were questioned by Judge Bonomy you said not that cluster bombs were the cause, you said that it could have led to population movements. Do you still agree with that testimony in Milutinovic, what you told Judge Bonomy, or are you giving us new testimony today that you know, in the last two years you have become certain, that this is what caused the population movements?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I said regarding cluster bombs and by what I said here today, but I claim on the basis of the knowledge I have two years later, on the basis of research that I have done with respect to depleted uranium, the number of sick people and the nature of the diseases that occur --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No, no, General, I'm not asking you about research into depleted uranium. I'm asking you specifically about your knowledge about why Albanians fled Kosovo. And to be clear, your additional research has been talking to a few ethnic Serb families who are your friends. That's your additional research, and based on that, you have strengthened your opinion that you know this is why Albanians left Kosovo. Is that -- is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this research, I had statistics of the number of people sick in the south of Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija. According to the data of the health centre in Kosovska Mitrovica and the statements of Rade Trajkovic, who is head of the medical centre, the number of people suffering from cancer of the liver, kidneys, the number of born children with defects has increased ten or more times. Now, in Kosovo and Metohija, one of the reasons, in my opinion, is the use of this type of ammunition. And to go back to your first question. Do you believe that when a container with a cluster bomb which contains 400 types of different cluster bombs, incendiary, et cetera, covers a territory of several hundred kilometres and if this explodes, if you listen to the fireworks during New Year's celebrations, then it can cause fear among people in a city. And when such a quantity of cluster bombs and the explosions that occur in the air, this certainly does provoke fear --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
