utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and it tends to lead to fleeing. That is the assessment of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: -- thank you, General, thank you, General. You've said a lot there. Just to deal with the first thing. So now you've said you've got a second piece of new information, which is that people were sick, people have gotten sick. You can agree, General, that this does nothing to explain why people would have fled -- why Albanians would have fled Kosovo in March of 1999, in April of 1999, in May of 1999, this data that later subsequently people have gotten sick. Those two things are not related; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This confirms our assertion and our knowledge and our warnings to the population which we gave in March and February 1999 to units in Kosovo, units of the army, the civil defence, and the population of the dangers threatening in the event of the use of depleted uranium munitions. Do you believe that any normal person would wait --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and stay in a radioactive area --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, I need you to answer the question that I am asking you. Can you agree with me that evidence of later sickness of people does nothing to tell us whether people were fleeing bombs in March of 1999, in April of 1999? It may have some relevance as to whether your fears were true, but it doesn't tell us why people were leaving. Can we agree on that and move on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that because I begin -- the beginning of the exodus was linked to the method, intensity, and type of bombing by NATO. This couldn't be done in a couple of days, as planned. Then they launched a general offensive and used all available munitions they had. And I claim in this court - whether you will admit it as evidence or not - that both use of cluster bombs and depleted uranium munitions were factors which prompted the population to flee --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- whether there were other reasons you will establish during the proceedings. I will not go into that, but I'm claiming that these two factors certainly contributed to the beginning of the population migrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what you said to Judge Bonomy is true, other than what you've told us today about talking to Serbian families and looking at data that people have gotten sick. What you told Judge Bonomy in the Milutinovic trial is true when he asked you: "You have done research on this, have you, the movement of the population as a result of the use of these cluster bombs?" And you told him: "I did not deal with that particular topic." Can you -- is that true, what you said to Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: That is true. That is what I said to Judge Bonomy, that is what I said. But today we are going further in the discussion, and I'm explaining. So I stand by what I'm saying now. These are my assessments and I stand by them. Now, whether from your standpoint or the standpoint of the Chamber, this is acceptable, it is up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, also in Milutinovic at that time you were careful to say that there could be other things, other causes, or other factors. You stated: "It is one of the factors that could have led to the population movements." Do you stand by that testimony today, or are you also changing this testimony? Do you stand by the testimony that there could have been other factors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about an assessment that I'm making here and that I stand by. This was one of the segments that could contribute to the movement of the population. I didn't enter into others.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just turn back to Exhibit 518, briefly, Defence Exhibit 518. So looking at this exhibit, by your own testimony you can see, we can see, that the heaviest missile strikes were right along the border with Albania. And, General, you've also conceded that people from all over -- Albanians from all over Kosovo, from many villages were fleeing out of Kosovo and many of them fled into Albania. My question to you is: Why would civilians flee bonds only towards -- to head straight towards an area of heavy missile strikes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the directions of the departure of civilians from Kosovo were not across the Prokletije mountains, but through Pec and Macedonia. So the areas that were struck were marked, those territories are still there and NATO forces, but they're not entering that area. They're haunted area. So these areas were marked, indicating: Warning, dangerous, risky. And as a unit there's a rule that you have to make a detour of these areas without crossing them because they're dangerous for survival. So if an inhabitant sees that this territory has been marked, he doesn't go across that territory, but in a round-about way, which will still make it possible for him to reach his destination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- a peasant -- a peasant doesn't think in the way a soldier does --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, assuming that after a strike has occurred and your units come in and they seal it off and they say "contaminated," assuming that that happens and that's the case, there is still a fair amount of time when these missiles are falling, the missiles with being shot. So is it your testimony that people -- this is a pretty large area of land. Is it your testimony that based on your information people did not flee through that area? Is that your knowledge of Albanians leaving Kosovo? Or -- I'm not sure I'm understanding what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not deal with the routes that the population took to withdraw from the territory of Kosovo to other countries; I was dealing with contaminated areas and tried to make it accessible, this information about contamination to all people, troops and civilians. But you have to go back into the mentality of the people of the time and think like they did. Nothing can help me here. I'm going to get to that area over there because it's safer there, and nothing's going to hold me back. This is how they thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at the transcript today, page 36, line 11, I just wanted to clarify something with you. You said: "So from that territory," meaning this territory that you've marked as radioactive, "the idea was to expel the civilian population and to only leave the units there so that in the event of land forces, the casualties would be reduced and we would in that way avoid condemnation by the international community which would expect a lot of casualties if the civilians had stayed there." So are you -- is it your testimony today that there was a plan to expel the civilian population from this area by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- well, what I said was in this context. It was NATO's assessment that the favourable routes for the incursion of their land forces in the territory of Kosovo would be from Albania, maybe two or three routes; and many more from the territory of Macedonia. And if they were to launch such an operation, they would first to remove the civilian population because when the tanks started rolling in and when Serbian forces are engaged, civilian population should be saved from harm, and this was one of the ways to do so. I'm not talking about plans on the part of the VJ. This was my presumption that this was one of the ways for NATO forces to clear the area without major casualties, so as to make that territory more favourable for the advance of NATO troops. Because had victims been effected in their launch, then that would lead to international condemnation of their actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clarifying that. And just briefly, did NATO bomb locations in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: By what? Belgrade was bombarded. You know, the MUP building, the state security department, Ministry of Defence, bridges in Novi Sad. Civilian targets were hit in Belgrade, in other towns, and settlements in former Yugoslavia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And do you agree that there was not a mass exodus of civilians from Belgrade like the ones seen in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. At the time I resided close to the facilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point my learned friend asked a question which is irrelevant, absolutely, concerning the bombing of Belgrade because we are discussing the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I do believe that this in no way can be subject matter for her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand the point being put to the witness is that bombing in the Belgrade area did not cause mass evacuation. And if that is the point, it may have some relevance. And the General was dealing with that point as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You can proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we realised that NATO was not choosey about its targets and that apart from their -- what they saw as legitimate targets as the Ministry of Defence building, they were --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just re-pose the question so we're clear. My question is a very simple one. Do you agree or not that there was not a mass exodus of civilians from Belgrade like the ones seen from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no mass exodus, but there were civilians fleeing Belgrade, relocating to other towns and to other countries. At the General Staff of the VJ, we had a plan to evacuate Belgrade if the nuclear institute of Vinca were targeted because we were aware of the hazard in the aftermath of such a bombing. So there was some movement of people, not en masse, but individual cases were recorded that people moved out of the areas that were targeted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So you'll agree, there was not movement en masse, some individual people may have left, but it was not en masse. Your testimony today is not that people left Belgrade to the same degree as Albanians left Kosovo; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you and say yes, but Belgrade was not bombarded to the same level as Kosovo was bombarded. Had it been bombarded at the same level, then it must -- it would have resulted in mass exodus.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So based on that, you would agree then that one cannot say as a rule: If bombs fall, civilians flee. You have to look at other factors, the degree of the bombing, for example. Just because bombs fell in general, civilians don't just flee. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that the only impetus comes from bombs falling. It's all about intensity of bombing. If the feeling of uncertainty is higher because of being somewhere, if the arsenal used is more diverse, if the level of security is lower then people will flee. Of course I'm not excluding other factors which may influence the movement of population, but this is one of the primary factors in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So there are many factors that could come in to play, and one would actually need to really look into those factors, do some research into it before one could conclude exactly why a population fled. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: You will most probably gather the big picture and the complete picture in this trial. I'm discussing one segment: The bombing of Kosovo and Metohija by certain -- with certain types of ammunition, hitting chemical plants and tanks and cluster bombs. I'm sure that you will find that what I said was one of the major influences in people moving around Kosovo and later on outside the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Petersen. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very short and brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of my questions, since we've broached the subject of the bombing of Belgrade, in that direction. General, sir, since you were in charge of ABH defence and then N, nuclear defence, if I may, during your examination-in-chief you confirmed that you notified subordinate units but also the civilians defence and the Territorial Defence on the threat that depleted uranium munition use would be posing. My specific question, since I believe that this parallel is inappropriate and useless, let me ask you: During the NATO aggression was there any case of depleted uranium or depleted uranium rounds were used in the territory of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: We had information that NATO forces had available Tomahawk cruise missiles and in the stabilising mechanism they contained 4 kilogrammes of uranium. But as I said in the case of Kosovo and Metohija we did have observation posts throughout Serbia. We found depleted uranium south of the 44th parallel in the areas of -- municipalities of Bujanovc, Presevo, et cetera. But in the territory of Belgrade, we did not find or confirm the presence of depleted uranium, either through laboratory tests or otherwise. And since the building of our General Staff was hit by cruise missiles, we tried to analyse samples there, but we have no proof that territory north of the 44th parallel was hit by depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Had you had such information you would have notified civil defence, Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by virtue of our position and duties, we had to do so. I explained that we worked intensively on preparing the population of Belgrade in the case the nuclear reactor within the Vinca institute, there are two of them, were bombarded, there is a certain amount of either used, spent, or stockpile of nuclear fuels there. Thank God this did not come about, but we had certain announcements that this may happen, and we prepared plans to notify the population. We prepared certain transport effects to take in place a plan to evacuate people if the institute had been bombed. And we had some estimates on the aftermath of the bombing of that institute. It -- had it been bombed, the results would be as if a 50-kilo tonne bomb had been detonated. Of course we made plans depending on the prevailing wind directions, et cetera, to evacuate people if that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You just answered part of my questions that I wanted to direct to you during -- concerning the cross-examination of my learned colleague. I have no further questions, and I thank you for your arrival here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just be clear, I think you were trying to make clear your concern at the possibility of an attack on the Vinca institute was because of a stockpile of -- that Serbia had of nuclear fuels in the institute; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can repeat the first portion of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've expressed clearly a number of contingency plans that you had and the General Staff had in the event of an attack on the Vinca institute. Is it Vinka or Vinca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It's nuclear institute Vinca, that is the name place, Vinca, next to Belgrade. Yes, we did have contingency plans and we thought what to do in case NATO bombarded the territory where the institute was located. And as I said, because of the character and the type of radioactive materials on that location, it would have resulted in a major disaster, a major catastrophe. And we had preparations for that, we notified the population what to do; but thank God this never occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Serbia had a nuclear reactor in that institute; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There were two nuclear reactors in that institute. One was operational and one was stopped and conservated. The one which was operational was used in fundamental research in terms of protection, detection, dosimetry, as far as I knew from the contacts I had with those people working in the institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the concern that you are expressing about such an attack was because of the stockpile of nuclear fuels that you had in the institute?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: For your information, there is -- there are uranium bars which are nuclear fuel within the reactor which are unspent. Then there is some fuel for the next stage on stockpile, and the third type of fuel was spent nuclear fuel which had to be stored in special warehouses. There was the official warehouse for radioactive waste for the whole Yugoslavia, which received radioactive medical spent fuel and other radioactive materials. And all the materials that were collected in Kosovo and Metohija during the war activities and from other parts of Serbia once war operations were over, we used that nuclear fuel warehouse to store those samples as well. So we -- threats came from both nuclear waste and nuclear fuel which was kept in that official nuclear materials warehouse at the institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that institute was not bombed or the subject of attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The institute was not bombed, but it was subject to manipulations in terms of announcement that it would be bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to get clear what was the basis of the concern you expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today you told us that you at least once went to Kosovo during the war to visit units of the 3rd Army and that you didn't have any contact or police units at that time. Could you be a little bit more precise, when exactly have you been in Kosovo during the war? What were the dates? And was it the only time, or have you been there several times?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this was the only time. I do not remember the dates. Trust me. I don't know that this would be a question put to me. I would have checked. It was in April. I visited units stationed in the area of Pec, and in that area -- this is the area I visited primarily because it was targeted heavily with DU munitions, and I found some vehicles that had been hit and marked as radioactive on the Djakovica-Pec road. Then I visited the front line units in the area of Kosara towards the Albania border. During my stay in Kosovo I did not encounter policemen or their officers or command staff. We visited the 3rd Army command post in Pristina. When we arrived there, people were then issued with tasks and missions and I was given the mission to go to Pec. I went there, went back to Belgrade, and reported back. During my stay there, I had no contacts with policemen. The only contacts I had were with troops in the area of Kosare close to the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have any contact with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, at the time I had no contacts with civilians. I dealt with problems of military nature prevalent in the units there. I did not have any time to spend on any civilian issues or issues of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you see any columns or groups of people leaving the villages in any direction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. During our arrival to Kosovo and en route from Kosovo to Pec and to the locale that we were supposed to visit, I did not see any columns of civilians during that trip and the trip back and while I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you get, during your stay in Kosovo, any information from people from -- you said you had contact to members of the army. Did you get any information about the reasons why people left their villages, their homes, and at least at the end, the country?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. Subject matter of my interest was what I was dealing with, and certain issues concerning control and command of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your preparedness to come to The Hague, for the assistance that you've been able to give, and you may of course now return to your normal activities. And a court officer will show you out. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, this is the last witness for today. Since, due to a misfortune at the beginning of last week, we had a witness ending up in ER concerning some cardiological problems. Our next witness, Mr. Krga, is going to be here on Monday and the Defence will be able to continue presenting its case on Monday, not earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Early in the case as it is and given the difficulties you've had, we accept what you say with a smile, Mr. Djordjevic, and we will continue the evidence on Monday. The Chamber, though, would draw attention to the fact that we have not only lost the whole of the three days available last week, but we have this week made very slow progress. The programme indicated by the Defence for its witnesses indicated that there would be five called, only three have. The programme indicated that two of the witnesses would be dealt with by an examination-in-chief of some two hours for each witness, and this witness for some one and a half hours. This witness went fairly quickly, but the two previous witnesses, their evidence stretched over four days rather than what might have been anticipated of less than two days. We bring this to attention now because if this rate of progress continues, this case will go to near the end of the year, and that's just not satisfactory. So we need to start moving quickly with Defence witnesses, just as we had to move quickly with Prosecution witnesses. Now, I'm sure that this is a matter that you will take under consideration, Mr. Djordjevic, and that efforts, effective efforts, will be made to deal with this and ensure that we really get moving through the case. Care needs to be taken that we only hear evidence that's really relevant and not waste time on incidental and [indiscernible] issues. And that if your questions and those of Mr. Djurdjic and your other colleagues are to the point, it will assist the Prosecution to be equally to the point in their cross-examination and we can see the progress starting to move as it should. If that can be the subject of attention by yourself and your colleagues as you move into the defence more seriously, we'd be very grateful. We've got to get the case moving again quickly in fairness to your client and everybody. We now adjourn, to resume tomorrow -- on Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
